reference_traces.rationale: Reviewer feedback identifies a narrower novelty boundary: exonucleolytic activity was reported for bacterial RNase HI, while the final paper distinguishes the yeast enzyme by its directionality and hybrid-binding context.

Reviewers described the combination of single-molecule approaches, directional cleavage, and RPA-enabled bidirectionality as the central mechanistic contribution; the final paper presents these observations and the integrated model.
The reviewer identified the optical-tweezer, fluorescence, smFRET, and gel evidence as a coherent experimental basis; the final paper specifies the complementary assays and quantitative sampling.
The reviewer’s account of directional RNase H1 activity is supported in the final paper by bead-size direction assignment, event counts, and rate/processivity measurements.

The final paper reports RNase H1 at active junctions and uses fluorophore disappearance from a forked substrate to assign 5′-to-3′ activity. Reviewers noted that these readouts do not by themselves exclude junction-proximal endonucleolytic cleavage followed by release.

Additional substrates and a nuclease-deficient mutant strengthen the unwinding interpretation, but the final 6-bp estimate still derives from three FRET increments under an explicit equal-step assumption.
The final discussion retains direct RNase H1–RPA interactions as a possible contributor, so the presented data do not isolate pre-separation as the sole mechanism of RPA stimulation.
The final paper proposes a spring-loaded mechanism powered by phosphodiester hydrolysis but presents it as a possible explanation rather than a directly tested energetic mechanism.

The final discussion extrapolates from nanomolar enzyme concentrations and long hybrids to cellular clearance, whereas direct cellular measurements of the proposed bidirectional mechanism are not presented.
Terminology concern is audit-only: the response states that “translocation” and “molecular motor” were replaced, and the final discussion uses the qualified term “motor-like.”
Reporting-completeness requests are audit-only: the response says event numbers were added, and the final Fig. 1 legend reports n for each concentration.

limiting_points.suggested_action: Frame novelty around the yeast enzyme’s directional mechanism and RPA-dependent context, rather than exonucleolytic activity in general.
limiting_points.text: Prior work on E. coli RNase HI limits any broad claim that RNase H exonucleolytic activity itself is unprecedented; the differentiated contribution is the scRNase H1 mechanism and directionality.

supporting_points.suggested_action: State the contribution as a single-molecule mechanistic account linking RPA or force-mediated hybrid pre-separation to bidirectional cleavage behavior.
supporting_points.text: The contribution is the mechanistic integration of directional RNase H1 cleavage with RPA-associated bidirectional events and hybrid pre-separation.

questions.suggested_action: Test or further delimit the proposed coupling between cleavage chemistry, elastic energy, unwinding, and directional movement.
questions.text: What direct evidence distinguishes the proposed spring-loaded energy-coupling mechanism from alternative explanations for directional movement?

questions.suggested_action: Assess whether the observed rates and RPA-dependent bidirectionality operate on cellular R-loops or in physiologically representative reconstitutions.
questions.text: How closely do the measured cleavage rates and bidirectional mechanism represent RNA–DNA hybrid clearance in vivo?

strengths.suggested_action: Retain the cross-assay linkage between force, fluorescence, smFRET, and product analyses.
strengths.text: Complementary optical-tweezer, confocal, smFRET, and gel assays connect molecular trajectories to cleavage-product and kinetic measurements.

strengths.suggested_action: Keep the directionality conclusion tied to the bead-size assignment, event count, and measured rate and processivity.
strengths.text: The directionality analysis uses distinguishable bead ends and reports all 20 observed events moving toward the predicted bead, alongside quantitative rate and processivity estimates.

summary.text: The paper uses single-molecule force, fluorescence, smFRET, and bulk assays to characterize S. cerevisiae RNase H1 cleavage of RNA–DNA hybrids. It advances a model in which 3′-to-5′ processive cleavage is coupled to hybrid unwinding and in which RPA or force-associated pre-separation permits bidirectional behavior. The central remaining limitations concern mechanistic assignment of the 5′ direction, precision of the proposed 6-bp step, and separation of RPA’s structural and direct-interaction effects.

weaknesses.suggested_action: Add an assay that resolves individual RNA cleavage positions or products at each active junction to distinguish terminal exonucleolysis from repeated junction-proximal endonucleolysis.
weaknesses.text: The 5′-to-3′ assignment remains indirect: junction-localized RNase H1 and fluorophore disappearance are compatible with the proposed activity but do not fully exclude repeated endonucleolytic cuts near the junction.

weaknesses.suggested_action: Quantitatively calibrate FRET states against independently defined unwound lengths and test unequal-step models.
weaknesses.text: The 6-bp unwinding model remains an inference: the final estimate divides a 17-nt transition across three FRET steps under an explicit equal-step assumption.

weaknesses.suggested_action: Separate RPA-driven hybrid pre-separation from direct RNase H1–RPA interactions using interaction-deficient or substrate-controlled experiments.
weaknesses.text: The data support hybrid pre-separation as a mechanism of RPA stimulation, but the final discussion also retains direct RNase H1–RPA interaction as a possible contributor, preventing an exclusive mechanistic attribution.

revision_ledger.residual_summary: The terminology request is reflected in the qualified final wording; the independently retained energetics question is tracked separately.
The final legend reports sample counts for the Fig. 1 concentration conditions.
